- When sentiment is consistently negative or neutral (e.g., 0.00 or low values), model tends to overcorrect downward; adjust forecast upward slightly to avoid underestimating rebound.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >90), model often overshoots and fails to account for subsequent mean reversion; reduce forecast slope or add early correction factor.
- If sentiment is positive and price is trending up, model may lag in recognizing momentum; increase forecast slope or add momentum multiplier.
- In low-sentiment periods with high historical volatility, model tends to underestimate volatility; add volatility buffer or widen forecast range.
- When sentiment is neutral and price is near historical mean, model often predicts flat trend; introduce slight upward bias to account for mean reversion bias.
- If model forecast is flat or trending down while sentiment is positive, reverse direction slightly to avoid sentiment mismatch.
- For 30-day horizon, model often underestimates late-period spikes; add late-period sensitivity factor (e.g., 10-15% weight on last 5 days).
